title: Model-driven analysis reveals oxidative stress adaptation enabling efficient energy utilization in a Crabtree-negative Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
projectDescription: The metabolic engineering of Saccharomyces cerevisiae to abolish the Crabtree effect via a pyruvate dehydrogenase bypass has enabled growth in minimal medium with glucose as the sole carbon source, although at a low growth rate. Adaptive laboratory evolution of the engineered strain (sZJD23), followed by reverse engineering, produced a variant (sZJD28) with significantly improved growth. This is mainly due to a mutation in MED2, which encodes a subunit of the mediator complex and, to a lesser extent, a mutation in GPD1, which encodes a glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase. Here, using quantitative proteomics and enzyme-constrained genome-scale modelling, we show that these mutations jointly enable a more efficient strategy for oxidative stress adaptation and energy utilization. Specifically, the MED2 mutation reshapes the oxidative stress response, including peroxisomal detoxification, while the GPD1 mutation suppresses a suboptimal redox-balancing strategy in the primary strain. Collectively, these changes result in improved flux distribution, lower protein costs in energy metabolism, and potentially enhanced ATP availability. Our findings reveal how specific mutations coordinate stress tolerance and metabolic efficiency to restore growth in engineered Crabtree-negative yeast.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Samples were suspended in lysis buffer containing 2% sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) and 50 mM triethylammonium bicarbonate (TEAB), and homogenized using lysis matrix on a FastPrep®-24 instrument (MP Biomedicals) for 4 repeated 40 second cycles at 6.5 m/s. Lysed samples were centrifuged at 16,200xg for 10 min and the supernatants were transferred to tubes. Protein concentrations in the lysates were determined. Aliquots containing equal protein amount from each sample were mixed to a reference sample. For the tandem mass tag (TMT) relative quantification experiment, aliquots containing 30 µg of total protein from each sample were incubated at 37°C for 60 min in the lysis buffer with DL-dithiothreitol (DTT) at 100 mM final concentration. The reduced samples were processed via the modified filter-aided sample preparation (FASP) protocol (Wisniewski JR et. al. Nat Methods. 2009 May;6(5):359-62). In short, the reduced samples were diluted to 1:4 by 8M urea, transferred onto Nanosep 30k Omega filters (Pall,) and washed repeatedly with 8 M urea and once with digestion buffer (DB) containing 0.5% sodium deoxycholate (SDC) and 50 mM TEAB. Free cysteine residues were modified using 10 mM methyl methanethiosulfonate (MMTS) solution in DB for 20 min at room temperature and the filters were washed twice with 100 µl of DB. Trypsin (Pierce MS Grade, Thermo Scientific) in digestion buffer was added at a ratio of 1:100 and the samples were incubated at 37°C o/n, then an additional 1:100 portion of trypsin was added and incubated for 3h. Peptides were collected by centrifugation and labeled using Tandem Mass Tag (TMT 10plex) reagents (Thermo Scientific) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The labeled samples were combined into one pool, concentrated using vacuum centrifugation, and SDC was removed by acidification with 10% TFA. The pool was treated with HiPPR detergent removal kit (Thermo Scientific) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. For the label-free quantification, a 50 µg aliquot of the pooled reference sample was mixed with 10.6 µg of the UPS2 Proteomics Dynamic Range Standard (Sigma-Aldrich), and the sample was digested with trypsin as above. Digested peptide sample was treated with HiPPR detergent removal kit as above. Peptides were fractionated via basic-pH reversed-phase chromatography on an XBridge BEH C18 column (3.5 μm, 3.0x150 mm, Waters) using a Dionex 3000 UPLC (Thermo Scientific), solvent A was 10 mM ammonium formate buffer at pH 10 and solvent B was 90% acetonitrile (ACN), 10% solvent A. Label-free sample was separated into 20 primary fractions. Primary fractions were concatenated into 10 final fractions. TMT-labeled peptides were fractionated into 40 primary fractions. The primary fractions were concatenated into 20 final fractions. The concatenated fractions were dried, and reconstituted in 15μl of 3% ACN, 0.2% formic acid (FA) for LCMS analysis. The TMT-labeled fractions (workflow 1) and the label-free fractions (workflow 2) were analyzed on an Orbitrap Fusion Lumos mass spectrometer interfaced with Easy-nLC 1200 liquid chromatography systems (both from Thermo Scientific). Peptides were trapped on an Acclaim Pepmap 100 C18 trap column (100 μm x 2 cm, particle size 5 μm, Thermo Scientific) and separated on an analytical column (75 μm x 35 cm, packed in-house with Reprosil-Pur C18, particle size 3 μm, Dr. Maisch) at 300 nL/min flow rate using 0.2% formic acid in water as solvent A and 80% ACN and 0.2% FA as solvent B. In workflow 1, peptides were eluted using the linear gradient from 5% to 33% B over 77 min. Full MS scans were performed at 120,000 resolution in the m/z range 375-1375. The most abundant 2-7 charged precursors from the MS1 scans were isolated using the quadrupole with 0.7 m/z isolation window with a “top speed” duty cycle of 3 s and dynamic exclusion within 10 ppm for 45 seconds, fragmented by collision induced dissociation (CID) at 35% collision energy with the max injection time of 50 ms, and the MS2 spectra were detected in the ion trap. Top 10 MS2 fragment ions within the m/z range 400-1400 were simultaneously isolated, fragmented by higher-energy collision dissociation (HCD) at 65% collision energy, and the MS3 spectra were recorded in the Orbitrap at 50,000 resolution, m/z range 100-500 and maximum injection time 105 ms. In workflow 2, each label-free fraction was injected in triplicate. Peptides were eluted using the linear gradient from 5% to 35% B over 105 min. MS1 scans were performed at 120 000 resolution in the m/z range 375-1375, the most abundant 2-7 charged precursors were isolated within 1.0 m/z window using the quadrupole with a “top speed” duty cycle of 3 s and dynamic exclusion within 10 ppm for 60 seconds. Precursors were fragmented using HCD at 30% collision energy and the MS2 spectra were recorded at 15,000 resolution with the max injection time of 100 ms and “Auto Normal” scan range.
dataProcessingProtocol: Proteome Discoverer version 2.4 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used for protein identification and quantification. Saccharomyces cerevisiae ATCC 204508 / S288c reference proteome database was downloaded from Uniprot (May 2020) and supplemented with the sequences of the proteins A0A100VDM2 and D4YIP5 and of the common proteomic contaminants; in the label-free workflow 2, the S. cerevisiae database was additionally supplemented with the sequences of the 48 UPS proteins. The following parameters were common between the workflows: Mascot version 2.5.1 (Matrix Science, London, UK) was used as a database search engine; 5 ppm precursor tolerance; trypsin with 1 allowed missed cleavage as an enzyme rule; oxidation on methionine as a variable modification; methylthiolation on cysteine as a fixed modification; Percolator for PSM validation with the strict FDR threshold of 1%. Additional parameters for the TMT workflow 1: fragment mass tolerance of 0.6 Da; TMT as a fixed modification on peptide N-termini and lysine; TMT 10plex Lot. No UF282324 as a quantification method with the reporters identified within 3 mmu in the MS3 spectra; quantification based on unique peptides and reporter S/N, with the correction for isotopic impurities, the average reporter S/N threshold of 10 and SPS match threshold of 40%; reporter normalization on total peptide amount. Additional parameters for the label-free workflow 2: precursor mass recalibration enabled with the initial precursor match tolerance of 15 ppm; fragment mass tolerance of 0.03 Da for the main search; Minora Feature detection was used for precursor ion quantification; intensities at peak maxima for the unique peptides were used for protein quantification; chromatographic retention time (RT) alignment was enabled with the max RT shift of 10 min; feature linking and mapping was enabled with the minimal S/N of 5. Protein intensities from 3 injection replicates were averaged. Modified intensity-based absolute quantification (IBAQ) approach [Schwanhausser, B. et al. Nature 473, 337–342 (2011). https://doi.org/10.1038/nature10098] was used to estimate the absolute protein amounts in the pooled reference sample: protein intensity was divided by the number of identified peptides to yield the IBAQ intensity for each protein; linear regression was calculated for the relationships between the known log10-transformed protein amount and measured log10-transformed IBAQ abundance on the spiked UPS2 standard proteins; the resulting regression model and measured IBAQ abundances of yeast proteins were used to estimate their protein amounts.
